title: I Spent Weeks With Keurig’s Posh, Plastic-Free Pod Coffee System: What Works and What Doesn’t
snippet: Alta is the brand’s first machine to brew 100% plastic-free pods. Here’s what I thought after weeks of testing.
fullText:
As a seasoned reviewer of all things coffee, I’ve sampled my fair share of Keurig products. After all, the brand’s presence is far-reaching; Keurig’s single-serve coffee makers are found in tens of millions of American households. So when I heard the brand had completely revamped its hard plastic-encased K-Cup, I knew this was big news. First teased way back in 2024, Keurig’s plastic-free pod coffee system has finally arrived.

	

		

	

									

									

						

	

				

			Nikita Ephanov/CNET		

	

		

									

						Keurig Alta					

					

	8.0

	
					

			

	

		

			

				Pros & Cons			

			

			

							

					
						The plastic-free pods are an achievement in themselves					
				

							

					
						The steam wand is high-quality					
				

							

					
						On balance, the coffee brewed was impressive					
				

							

					
						The digital interface was easy to use					
				

					

			

							

					
						Individual AltaRounds are packaged in plastic (for now)					
				

							

					
						Keurig's largest coffee brewer, it takes up a good deal of counter space					
				

							

					
						The price is steep					
				

							

					
						The espresso lacked some body					
				

					

	

		

Called an AltaRound, this puck consists of coffee grounds encased in seaweed-derived gel. The changes go beyond packaging. The transformed pods come with a new machine, the Alta, a revamped brewer that marks Keurig’s first foray into high-pressure espresso extraction. The machine extracts at up to 10 bars, on par with a standard espresso machine.

Put the puck and coffee machine together, and the technology is striking. The coffee maker even scans QR codes printed on the pucks and suggests drinks on a touchscreen. It’s a futuristic reinvention, but what matters most to me is the environmental initiative coupled with coffee quality. It’s an ambitious redesign on Keurig’s consumer scale; I couldn’t wait to see how the new Alta system performs.

			

More from CNET

The Keurig Alta Brewer is sizable yet stylish

It’s a commitment in both cost and counter space.Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Keurig’s range of coffee makers spans from no-frills single-button models to spiffed-up machines. Right out of the box, the Alta is clearly the brand’s most substantial offering yet. The appliance is fairly large, taking up 19 inches by 10 inches of counter space and standing 1 foot tall. The back has a removable 70-ounce water tank, while the front has a steam wand and pitcher.

	

			

	

			

									

						The 4 Best Pod Coffee Makers We Tested					

							

		

You deposit pods into the top of the machine, directly under an electronic display, so you’ll need 8 more inches of vertical clearance to operate. Spent pucks and liquids collect in a compartment on the machine’s left side. With so many moving parts, the coffeemaker needs ample counter space. I also found the cord on the short side, so plan its placement accordingly.

As of this writing,  you can buy Light, Medium, and Dark Roast pucks.Nikita Ephanov/CNET

The aesthetics make up for the size. The Keurig Alta looks more like a retro espresso maker than a pod machine. I’m a fan of the smooth, lightly ’70s-inspired shape and the bright white color. The absence of a single button or immediately noticeable display adds to the sleekness. Brewing functions are controlled via a compact digital screen on top of the brewer, roughly the size of a smartphone.

To set it up, the machine syncs to Wi-Fi, and the touchscreen guides the initial configuration. The display enhances the Keurig’s already intuitive process. Each Alta puck comes stamped with a QR code the coffee maker scans, which prompts several suggested beverages. The coffee maker feels like an expanded and modernized Keurig experience. At $500, though, I’d expect all the bells and whistles.   

The touchscreen gave me no grief.Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Hands-on with the new Keurig Alta pods

Keurig’s new machine is certainly eye-catching, but the accompanying AltaRounds are the real headline. I’ve never handled a coffee product quite like them. Each 14-gram pod resembles a damp espresso puck, yet comes bound with a thin, NSF-certified seaweed film. The material isn’t brittle, so I can pick up an AltaRound and drop it into the brewer with my fingers without worrying about loose grounds. Remarkably, the pucks remain intact even after extraction, altered only by a handful of needle-like piercings. 

Compared to the hard plastic-encased K-Cup, it’s a system built with sustainability in mind. Still, I don’t love that every AltaRound is sold in a non-recyclable plastic wrapper. A Keurig rep told me paper-based packaging is coming, but for now, the system generates more waste than a simple filter coffee.

Plastic-free pods wrapped in seaweed byproduct are the star of the show.Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Sampling the Keurig Alta’s coffee lineup

The newly debuted AltaRound lineup is narrow, but all entirely new to the Keurig ecosystem. As of October 2026,  you can buy Light, Medium, and Dark Roast pucks, plus a sole flavored Caramel option. Additional options are in the works. Conveniently, the coffee maker also has a slot for older-generation plastic pods, so you can still brew your favorite K-Cups without committing to the new system.

The pods come in plastic packaging, though the brand plans to switch to paper wrappers soon.

The Alta brews a broad range of beverages, from thick, short espresso to foamy lattes or a standard mug of drip. No barista skills are required: The machine scans each pod, recommends a drink, then automates extraction. Even the milk frother is machine-driven, using a magnetic spinner at the bottom of the pitcher to help time and foam dairy. 

There is some room for customization, though. You can also froth manually, and adjust coffee to three strengths, temperatures, and sizes. You can also use the steam wand to make cold foam or hot froth. Keurig even offers suggested recipes for more complex drinks, like an espresso martini or salted caramel latte. There’s a lot to sample, and it can take several AltaRounds to find your preferred beverage. 

The steam wand worked well in my testing.Nikita Ephanov/CNET

I was most impressed by the double-shot dark roast, which brewed opaque and capped with an aesthetic crema, unlike any K-Cup I’ve brewed. Mixed with steamed milk, it yielded a tasty cappuccino, latte and cortado, approaching espresso machine caliber. 

Compared to conventional espresso, the coffee lacked some body, a sensory experience my testing confirmed. Both the single shot and double-shot AltaRounds weighed just shy of 14 grams. The latter produced some 98 grams of coffee, making it a 1:7 ratio far from the ideal 1:2 espresso shot. The dark roast AltaRound tastes pleasantly bold and bitter, but has neither the acidity nor concentrated flavor I’d expect from a barista-quality shot. It’s not true espresso, but considering the ease of brewing and shelf stability (nine months sealed, 30 days opened), I’d be happy to drink it.

The coffee was one-note but perfectly pleasant.Nikita Ephanov/CNET

The light and medium roast Alta pods appealed less to me. Brewed into a hot 8-ounce cup (the recommended preparation), both pods delivered more acidity, and the light roast added a touch of fruitiness. While brighter, the two coffees tasted bland, with a flat flavor. 

The cups also had a faintly woody, off-putting note, extra pronounced in the medium roast. Served iced, this tasting note intensified. The Keurig Alta lowers the extraction temperature for cold beverages, and this adjustment doesn’t bring out the best of AltaRounds. Mixing either roast profile with milk softens the issue; still, I generally preferred this machine for hot beverages. 

I liked the caramel AltaRound more, even though I don’t often sweeten my coffee. Blending sweet and toasted flavors, this puck successfully recreates a housemade syrup experience, especially in a hot drink with milk. Like the other pucks, the underlying coffee flavor is one-note but pleasant, making it a cup I’d sip every now and then. 

Overall, I didn’t find the brewed AltaRound coffees a significant improvement over K-Cups in flavor, though the coffee maker’s options are certainly far more comprehensive than previous models.

My verdict on the Keurig Alta 

If you’re a longtime Keurig user, the Alta is a significant revamp. The system delivers espresso-like brewing, a sleek machine, and the redesigned AltaRound. I’m all for more environmentally conscious coffee brewing, and this packaging is a step forward for single-serve coffee (plastic wrapper aside). The Alta arrives not long after Lavazza’s plastic-free pod system, and I welcome Keurig’s contribution to brewing waste reduction.

The price may be hard to swallow for casual coffee drinkers.Nikita Ephanov/CNET

The brand’s innovation does come at a steep price, though. The new brewer set costs $500 (including 32 AltaRounds to start), a step up from K-Cup brewers available for as low as $50. Puck refills are sold at $11 per eight-count box, discounted $1.50 a box when opting for the AutoRefresh subscription. Even at the lower price, that still works out to over $1 a cup. That’s pricier than making coffee at home using a drip machine, for example. 

In my opinion, the coffee flavors don’t warrant the increased cost. At this price, I’d opt for an automatic drip brewer or a semi-automated espresso machine, both of which let you use fresh coffee beans. However, if you want the convenience of shelf-stable pods for espresso drinks while staying loyal to Keurig coffee, the Alta is a worthwhile redesign.

title: iOS 27.2 just upgraded Apple Photos in two ways, here’s what’s new
snippet: Apple Photos got a lot of new features in iOS 27 last month, but this week’s release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
Apple Photos got a lot of new features in iOS 27 last month, but this week’s release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new.

Shared Albums are among my favorite features in the Photos app. I don’t post on social media often, but I love using Shared Albums because they provide a social media-style experience in a private way that lives right inside Photos.

iOS 27 brought a variety of big improvements to Shared Albums. And now iOS 27.2 has introduced four more. 

Per Apple’s release notes, here’s what’s new:

you can now edit captions for your photos and videos

comments can be edited too

there’s a feature to prevent adding duplicate photos to an album

the app can display a reminder before albums expire, so participants can save photos before they’re gone

To get these new features, you’ll need to make sure your Shared Albums have been upgraded for iOS 27.

#2: SynthID watermarking to identify AI-modified photos

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated. 

This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.

Apple is tackling the issue with its new Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Per Apple, its latest software update adds the following:

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground

SynthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. Users won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.

title: Anduril now says its BlueChip laptop will meet Buy American standards at launch
snippet: On Tuesday, defense contractor Anduril and chipmaker Qualcomm announced a partnership to build laptops entirely in the United States, starting with a single model in 2027. They also announced a "long-term goal" of pushing the computer industry to create "a fully domestic supply chain." Even a single Made-in-USA laptop would be a surprise, because no major US computer company builds its laptops here - not Apple, not Dell, not HP, not Microsoft. We're not aware of any company that does. But we are aware of companies that have briefly and strategically assembled computers here seemingly to appease President Donald Trump. We're also aware of … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
On Tuesday, defense contractor Anduril and chipmaker Qualcomm announced a partnership to build laptops entirely in the United States, starting with a single model in 2027. They also announced a “long-term goal” of pushing the computer industry to create “a fully domestic supply chain.”

Even a single Made-in-USA laptop would be a surprise, because no major US computer company builds its laptops here — not Apple, not Dell, not HP, not Microsoft. We’re not aware of any company that does.

But we are aware of companies that have briefly and strategically assembled computers here seemingly to appease President Donald Trump. We’re also aware of companies that have promised US jobs only to deliver empty buildings. And we’re aware of at least one fake “US” company that lied to the government about making product domestically.

That’s why we now ask pointed questions when a company says it’s committed to US manufacturing. We asked TP-Link those sorts of questions just over a week ago. On Monday, we asked Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Qualcomm president and CEO Cristiano Amon those kinds of questions.

Over the course of two days, Anduril has changed one important answer.

Anduril communications VP Shannon Prior now says the company’s laptop will have at least 65 percent of its components made in the US by the time it launches in 2027. It’s an important number, and one that Anduril did not commit to earlier this week.

Luckey held a call with reporters on Monday, during which he was clear that he wants to make literally every part of a computer in the United States — and that Anduril and Qualcomm have already mapped out a plan. “We have a technical roadmap to get to 100 percent domestic over time,” he told journalists.

Luckey also suggested his laptop would be built to comply with the requirements of the military and other government agencies — and that it would meet or exceed one specific US government standard that has an exact definition.

“We are not just barely meeting the bar for Made in America. We are going hard to make this an all-American play, and not even the Buy American Act requires what we’re trying,” Luckey said.

The Buy American Act dates back to 1933, but it was updated during the Biden Administration to require that at least 65 percent of the cost of a product’s components must be made domestically for it be considered a domestic product itself. That number is going up to 75 percent in 2029.

Many products need to be made in America to those standards, or federal agencies can’t buy them without receiving a waiver — which agencies currently use en masse, Luckey himself argued on the call. “There’s a number of government agencies that are required by law to buy American-made computers [...] All of those procurements are happening under waivers of those laws,” he said.

We also noticed that Anduril’s press release specifies that its first laptop will be “designed and assembled” in the United States, not necessarily “manufactured” here (though the release does talk about future manufacturing). This was also a sticking point with router maker TP-Link, which would not confirm full manufacturing even after suggesting it in an interview with The Verge.

That’s why we asked Luckey what percent of his first laptop’s components would be made in the US. His reply was not 65 percent or 70 percent. It was “TBD.” You can read the exchange for yourself:

The Verge: When it arrives in 2027, what percent of the components in the BlueChip laptop will be made in the US?

Luckey: TBD. I’m doing my very, very best. It’s gonna be a whole mix of things based on when do certain memory fabs come online? When do certain CPU, GPU fabs come online? There’s a whole— Like, am I able to get a display line here or not? Do I have to do that after launch? I’m being totally open kimono with you here. Those questions are not settled. It is not clear if I will be able. I know the glass is gonna be made in the US, I know the frame is gonna be made in the US around that display. I know that parts of the ribbon component are gonna be made in the U.S. I don’t know if I will have successfully pulled that component in or a dozen other components. So it’s a little up in the air. I’m doing my very, very best. I think most likely the thing that we ship is not going to be 100-percent American. I think it’ll be a blend of US and allies around the world, mostly US, probably a few things from some allies, and then that’ll be in the context of conversations with those allies about bringing those components into production in the United States, and I’m being honest with the government on this too. I mean, I’ve had conversations where I’ve said, listen. I would love to give you guys an American, 100-percent American laptop right off the bat, but that is not the environment the US government has created or US industry has created. I can’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good.

When we followed up by email to ask specifically about 65 percent, the answer was that the laptop prototype is currently at 32 percent and Anduril could not yet commit to 65 percent. Here’s Anduril spokesperson Stephanie Davis’ full reply on Tuesday:

For the prototype today, approximately 32% is U.S.-origin by component procurement cost, and more than 90% is sourced from the United States and allied countries combined.

We’re working to expand domestic sourcing and production ahead of planned availability in 2027, with the goal of eliminating foreign content and ultimately establishing an end-to-end American supply chain.

The final domestic-content percentage at launch remains unsettled, so we can’t confirm above or below 65% today. That’s why we’re asking you to revise the assertion that it will be “well below” that threshold.

Today, Prior writes that Anduril can indeed commit to 65 percent. Here is the most recent statement:

Our previous response to The Verge was incorrect. The BlueChip laptop is indeed being developed to exceed the 65% U.S. domestic-content threshold at launch in 2027. Meeting that threshold is a fundamental objective of the program. The precise domestic-content percentage of the final product is still being determined as we finalize suppliers and work through prototypes, and we look forward to sharing more next year.

Today’s statement is the first time Anduril has confirmed that we, and government agencies, theoretically shouldn’t need to wait until Anduril achieves its full goals to see a laptop that meets the Buy American standard. If everything works out, Anduril’s first laptop in 2027, with Qualcomm, should be that laptop.

We invited Luckey to explain how Anduril would get to 65 percent domestic component production in a follow-up interview, but we were told he’s not currently available. On the Monday call, he told journalists that Anduril already has a US glassmaker lined up for the laptop’s cover glass, is programming FPGAs (field-programmable gate arrays) to serve the purpose of power management chips and other circuits it can’t normally can’t get outside China, and is developing made-in-America batteries as well.

The press release adds that the enclosure is designed “for US machining” and the laptop will use metals “that US industry can produce and machine at scale.”

As for the laptop’s Snapdragon processor, we asked Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon about that. “TSMC has a manufacturing facility in Arizona, and that’s where our chips are going to be made,” he told The Verge.

Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

title: Amazon’s New Digital Picture Frame Is Clever and Classy
snippet: The frame, available in real wood finishes, is the first-ever with Amazon Alexa built in and offers unlimited storage for Prime members.
fullText:
Amazon just dropped its first-ever digital picture frame, right in time for the holiday gifting rush, along with a whole batch of new Echo-based gadgets. We got a peek at the Alexa Photo Frame at a launch event in New York, and it has a few neat tricks and design touches you won’t find on most frames.

The big standout is that the frame syncs automatically with Amazon Photos and picks out the “best” shots for you, so you’re not stuck watching all 300 photos from your upstate leaf-peeping trip on repeat. We love the idea, but we haven’t tested it yet, so we can’t say how well it curates.

	

			

	

			

									

						Smart Home Gift Buying Guide 2026: Upgrades Everyone Will Love					

							

		

The first smart frame with Alexa built in

Alexa prompts fetch the exact photos or photo types you want to see. 

Amazon’s frame, which comes with unlimited storage for Prime members, is the first with Alexa built in, so you can ask to see photos of certain people, places or events.

			

More from CNET

“Alexa, nobody believes me that I met Dolly Parton at Costco; please bring up the selfie,” is one example for locating photos.

You can also use AI-style prompts to create a specific slideshow, such as “show pictures of the kids” or “absolutely no pictures of the kids, please.” 

We’ve tested generative AI frames before, and most left us wanting more. SwitchBot recently came out with a second-gen AI frame model, but we haven’t seen anything like this Alexa hybrid approach before, which makes us really want to try it out.

High-definition picture that adjusts to changing light

Brightness automatically adjusts as ambient light changes.Amazon

The 10-inch high-definition, semi-matte, anti-glare finish was impressive, making photos look more like a physical photo than a screen, and they show clearly from almost any angle. A clever light sensor automatically adjusts the screen brightness from day to night.

The wood frame may be the best part

The frame comes in birch or walnut wood.

What first caught our eye was the textured, soft-white matting and the real wood frames, available in walnut, lighter birch or black. If you’ve browsed digital frames online, you’ve likely noticed a trend: drab black plastic designs with little warmth or visual appeal. Amazon’s wood options are a welcome departure from the norm, even if they cost more.

You can add voice notes to photos for some reason

Perhaps the strangest feature is the ability to add voice notes to accompany images as they pass across the screen to “capture the story behind the moment.” I suppose this might enhance the picture-frame experience in some cases, but I can’t think of many. 

Pricing and availability

The frame comes in three finishes, including two wood options, and begins shipping Dec. 16.Amazon

The Alexa Photo Frame is available starting today. It costs $200 for black plastic and $229 in one of two wood finishes, walnut or birch.

title: Amazon’s New Alarm Clock ‘Knows’ if You’re in a Deep Sleep and Lets You Sleep Longer
snippet: The Amazon Echo Time, launched today, has a few wild features.
fullText:
Amazon is revamping its smart home devices, and it’s adding a new smart alarm clock to the lineup for the first time. Called the Amazon Echo Time, this alarm clock with unique AI sleep features is designed specifically for bedrooms — and bucking Big Tech’s “pervert tech” trend, it includes no cameras. It’s available now for $200 and starts shipping in December.

Amazon’s first clock is smart and customizable

The Echo Time looks like a regular Alexa speaker with one key difference: a 3.2-inch screen. You can customize the display to show an analog or digital clock, including themed variants from popular franchises, like Harry Potter, the DC Universe and Scooby-Doo. It’s one of many devices that Amazon dropped on Wednesday, including a revamped Echo Show, Echo Studio and a first-ever smart picture frame.

Customize the display to show an analog or digital clock and use popular themes including Harry Potter, the DC Universe and Scooby-Doo.David Carnoy/CNET

Inside, the device uses tech that adapts to your daily routines. For example, it can gradually get brighter in the morning to support your wake-up routine and reduce blue light at night to help you fall asleep. Those features are similar to other smart clocks, like the popular Hatch Sleep Clock. The clock also comes in two versions built specifically for kids, with controls parents can use, including Amazon’s Sleep Studio for bedtime-routine management.

			

More from CNET

A wild (opt-in) AI feature pushes the alarm back if you’re in a deep sleep

Like nearly every piece of tech these days, the Echo Time has optional AI features. If you don’t need to jump out of bed at a certain time, you can let the Echo Time handle your alarm. The clock then uses sensors that monitor room temperature and movement, including ultrasonic detectors for your breathing, to decide when to wake you. It works within a 60-minute window around your wake-up time, letting you get a deep sleep or waking you early if it detects your sleep is no longer “restful.”

If that sounds creepy or like something that will make you run late in the morning, don’t worry: It’s optional, and it requires an Alexa Plus subscription.

The new Echo Time clocks come in graphite, glacier white and coral pink for adults, with galactic grape and cosmic lime options for kids.David Carnoy/CNET

While this feature could be dangerous during workdays or before a flight, it sounds perfect for sleepy weekends when you’re trying to catch up on rest. 

There have never been more smart home tech options. Earlier this month, Apple revamped its options and introduced a brand-new device called the Home View. Apple’s new devices impressed CNET reviewers, particularly with their easy-to-use setup. But families that already use Amazon devices will likely want to stay within the same ecosystem.

title: MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR vs MacBook Pro: Here’s every difference
snippet: Apple just unveiled its new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, which joins the lineup alongside the existing MacBook Pro using the same M5 Pro and Max chips. Here’s an in-depth comparison of the two models. more…
fullText:
Apple just unveiled its new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, which joins the lineup alongside the existing MacBook Pro using the same M5 Pro and Max chips. Here’s an in-depth comparison of the two models.

Design, size, and weight: PROLED XDR is thinner, lighter

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR has an all-new industrial design. It’s the first design overhaul for the MacBook Pro since 2021.

You still get a 14.2-inch regardless of whether you choose PROLED XDR or not. On the 16-inch model, PROLED XDR is 16.3 inches, slightly larger than the standard 16.2-inch.

Apple’s new design is a bit sleeker and significantly lighter-weight. It also brings back the glowing Apple logo on the lid that was an iconic element in previous generations. Additionally, the PROLED XDR has a newly designed hinge that provides greater stability.

Here’s a breakdown of how each model compares in size and weight:

PROLED XDR 14-inch

MacBook Pro 14-inch

PROLED XDR 16-inch

MacBook Pro 16-inch

Weight

3.0 pounds

3.5 pounds

4.0 pounds

4.7 pounds

Height

0.59 inch

0.61 inch

0.63 inch

0.66 inch

Width

12.24 inches

12.31 inches

14.0 inches

14.01 inches

Depth

8.52 inches

8.71 inches

9.62 inches

9.77 inches

As the numbers show, the overall size difference is fairly minor, but the reduced weight should be obvious to anyone who upgrades.

Display: Touchscreen PROLED XDR with Dynamic Island vs Mini-LED with notch

The new MacBook Pro’s display technology is so important, Apple put it in the branding. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR features a tandem OLED that Apple says is “the world’s best laptop display.”

Again, it’s available in 14.2-inch or 16.3-inch sizes that are nearly identical to the standard MacBook Pro.

The PROLED XDR display is touch-enabled, with macOS 27 introducing a variety of optimizations for touch input. So if you want a touchscreen on your Mac, that’s a big advantage.

Tandem OLED means you’ll get deeper blacks, true-to-life color, and also a new max peak brightness of 2,000 nits (up from 1,600). And Adobe RGB is now supported, along with a host of industry-standard reference modes.

There’s also a Dynamic Island on the new MacBook Pro. It replaces the notch and serves as the home to software features like Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI.

Performance and memory: M5 Pro and M5 Max chips

Apple is using the exact same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips in its two MacBook Pros, so performance should in theory be the same across models.

That said, real-world testing will reveal whether the new MacBook Pro design has an impact on sustained performance—for better or worse.

Memory options are also identical with the PROLED XDR model and standard MacBook Pro. That means:

M5 Pro models start at 24GB of RAM, with options for 48GB and 64GB

M5 Max models start at 36GB of RAM, with options for 48GB, 64GB, and 128GB

Storage: New 16TB option

MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR largely retains the same storage options as the standard MacBook Pro, with one exception.

M5 Pro models start at 1TB, with options for 2TB and 4TB

M5 Max models start at 2TB, with options for 4TB, 8TB, and 16TB

The only change here is that there’s now a high-end 16TB option when you choose M5 Max. Previously, 8TB was the most storage available in any MacBook Pro.

Battery and charging: Identical in every way

MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR offers identical battery life and fast charging features as the standard MacBook Pro. That means:

14-inch: up to 22 hours with M5 Pro, or 20 hours with M5 Max

16-inch: up to 24 hours with M5 Pro, or 22 hours with M5 Max

All MacBook Pro models can fast charge up to 50 percent battery in 30 minutes.

Camera: Advanced Video Stabilization

Apple’s MacBook Pro models all feature the same 12MP Center Stage camera with support for Desk View, 1080p HD video recording, and an advanced image signal processor with computational video.

However, because of touchscreen support, the PROLED XDR model adds one new feature: Advanced Video Stabilization.

Essentially, this exists so that if you’re touching your display during a video call, it won’t have an impact on your camera feed.

Speakers: All-new woofer design and closed-lid upgrades

The MacBook Pro PROLED XDR features largely the same speaker system as the standard model, but with a pair of key upgrades. Per Apple Newsroom:

The industry-leading six-speaker audio system in the new MacBook Pro features an all-new woofer design that provides 50 percent deeper bass and all-new tweeters that shape sound dispersion for remarkable clarity…And for the first time, dedicated audio tuning for closed-lid use delivers exceptional sound quality when MacBook Pro is connected to an external display, so users can enjoy a premium audio experience however they work.

Ports: All the same across models, with one small upgrade

Apple clearly learned from past mistakes of removing ports from pro users. With the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, you get all the same ports as on the standard MacBook Pro. Ports include:

SDXC card slot

HDMI port

3.5 mm headphone jack

MagSafe 3 port

Three Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C) ports with support for:

Charging

DisplayPort

Thunderbolt 5 (up to 120Gb/s)

USB 4 (up to 120Gb/s)

One upgrade that will benefit some users is that Genlock is now supported by the Thunderbolt 5 ports as well.

Pricing: PROLED XDR adds $400 premium

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399 for the 16-inch. That’s a $400 premium over the standard MacBook Pro.

title: Amazon’s latest Echo smart displays and speakers reinforce Google Home’s lost lead
snippet: Amazon just launched a new lineup of Echo smart speakers and a new smart display, all while Google Home’s lineup remains pretty quiet. more…
fullText:
Amazon just launched a new lineup of Echo smart speakers and a new smart display, all while Google Home’s lineup remains pretty quiet.

Amazon has five new devices launching – two smart displays, a “Photo Frame,” and two speakers.

Starting with the speakers, the latest Echo Dot has “a built-in smart home hub” and upgraded audio and starts shipping today for $100. Meanwhile, Echo Studio builds on that foundation with even-better audio and, optionally, a built-in camera. Those start at $220.

Echo Dot at Amazon (shipping now)

Echo Studio at Amazon (shipping now)

On the smart display side, there’s the Echo Time, which is like an Echo Dot but with a small circular display built-in. Amazon touts “hundreds of clock faces” and “Omnisense” which can track your sleep just like Google’s second-gen Nest Hub, and it starts at $200. 

	

Echo Show 16, meanwhile, is a big 16-inch smart display meant to live on your wall with support for smart home controls, the ability to show a family calendar, and full Fire TV built-in as well. It starts at $500 and, like everything else mentioned so far, is built around Amazon’s AI-enhanced Alexa.

Echo Time at Amazon (shipping now)

Echo Show 16 at Amazon (pre-order for $100 off, shipping December 16)

Rounding out the lineup is the Alexa Photo Frame, a simpler smart display that has Alexa built-in but focuses on showing photos from your Amazon Photos library. It has a 10-inch anti-glare display and a design that looks like a normal photo frame and starts at $200.

Alexa Photo Frame at Amazon (shipping now)

9to5Google’s Take

Google Home really is just so wildly behind isn’t it.

In looking at Amazon’s lineup, I can’t help but feel like Google is just wasting potential here. A smart speaker that doubles as a Nest Cam would be awesome. The same goes for a giant Nest Hub that doubles as a Google TV. 

	

And, seriously, how does Google not sell (or at least partner with someone) a Google Photos digital photo frame. Google Photos is a wildly successful platform and that would sell like hotcakes. Big “how am I not in that movie” energy.

I’ve said it before, but Google Home had such a lead in the smart speaker and smart display market, especially with Google’s ecosystem tie-ins, but Amazon is currently running laps around it with products that Google should be selling. Throw in that even Apple has a smart display now where Google hasn’t even teased a new Nest Hub, and it just feels all kinds of bad to be in Google’s camp right now.

What do you think?

title: Chrome 156 for Googlebook rolling out with 14 updates across sites, shortcuts, more
snippet: Google is rolling out Chrome 156 for Googlebooks with a slew of improvements and bug fixes. This follows the last browser update two weeks ago. more…
fullText:
Google is rolling out Chrome 156 for Googlebooks with a slew of improvements and bug fixes. This follows the last browser update two weeks ago.

In terms of “New Features,” there’s “Hover Tooltips in the AI Mode Menu: Items in the address bar’s AI Mode menu now show tooltips on mouse hover.”

The remaining 13 updates today are classified as “Improvements.” On the keyboard shortcuts front:

Alt+Tab: Alt+Tab now switches windows on Fullscreen sites and apps when keyboard lock is on, as it does on ChromeOS, Mac and Windows. Users no longer need to hold Esc to exit before switching tabs.

Alt+Shift+Enter Shortcut: Alt+Shift+Enter now opens the typed query in a new background tab and keeps you on the current page.

Up/Down Arrows in Multi-Line Address Bar Text: Up/Down arrows now move the cursor between lines for easier editing when typed text wraps to multiple lines. Suggestions are hidden.

Specific website improvements include:

	

Google Docs: Enabled copying of large selections and tables in Google Docs. 

Facebook Live Video: Performance improvement of Facebook Live streams.

Stability fixes: Stability improvements were made across 1Password and other extensions, third party apps, and Chrome tab functionality.

Site Icons: Site and Google icons appear correctly when clicking into the address bar from a webpage or search results page. Stale site icons are removed when the URL bar is cleared.

There are some meaningful usability fixes:

Close Third-Party Sign-In Prompts: The close (X) button will close third-party sign-in prompts correctly. 

File Downloads: Added “Save As” dialog support to choose download save locations, and fixed a naming issue with duplicate file downloads so they open correctly in apps.

Right-Click on Incognito New Tab Page: Context menu now opens when right-clicking links on the Incognito new tab page.

Finally, the AI Mode updates continue with:

AI Mode Animation Timing: The AI Mode animation waits for the expansion to complete before playing and plays more consistently.

“Add to your search”: The menu for adding tabs and files to an AI Mode search now has an “Add to your search” header.

“View your AI Mode history”: The address bar now correctly displays “Ask anything” hint text and blinking cursor.

We’re seeing Chrome 156 for Googlebook OS widely rolling out via the Play Store today. It comes a week after the stable release started on desktop and mobile (not fully available for Android phones and tablets yet).

title: iOS 27.2 has two CarPlay improvements, here’s what’s new
snippet: iOS 27.2 arrived this week with new features for Messages, Apple TV, and more, plus two improvements for CarPlay. Here’s what’s new for CarPlay users. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 arrived this week with new features for Messages, Apple TV, and more, plus two improvements for CarPlay. Here’s what’s new for CarPlay users.

#1: Apple Podcasts adds sections for New Episodes and Continue Playing

Apple Podcasts in iOS 27.2 adds two new sections to the Home tab: ‘New Episodes’ and ‘Continue Playing.’

Essentially, Apple has rethought how the core ‘Up Next’ queue of its Podcasts app works.

Like you would expect, ‘New Episodes’ contains only the latest episodes from your favorite shows. But after you’ve started an episode, you’ll find it in the ‘Continue Playing’ row just below.

This overhaul to podcast management makes it easier to find the latest episodes of your shows and also pick up where you previously left off. I’m a big fan of the change.

#2: Siri AI upgrades

Siri AI introduces a variety of upgrades in iOS 27.2, including two that carry over to CarPlay as well.

Per Apple’s release notes:

Siri AI can recall your past conversations, so you can ask Siri about something it told you before, like the restaurants it recommended last week

Siri AI can draw from more sources to give you a great answer, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, your voicemails, and better results from Safari history and Reading List

It can take some adjustment to remember that Siri AI is available in the car just like on iPhone. But CarPlay is an especially useful platform for Apple’s more powerful assistant.

Bonus: Apple Music’s new app icon and design tweaks

	

It’s arguable whether this qualifies as an “improvement,” but it is a change worth mentioning. iOS 27.2 includes a new app icon for Apple Music, plus some minor design tweaks in the app.

These changes are related to the total rebrand Apple Music unveiled just last week.

title: iOS 27.2 adds new Messages feature that’s already a favorite
snippet: iOS 27.2 launched this week with many new features for iPhone users, including a Messages addition that was previously announced for iOS 27 but later got pushed back: Suggestions. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 launched this week with many new features for iPhone users, including a Messages addition that was previously announced for iOS 27 but later got pushed back: Suggestions.

Messages ‘Suggestions’ return in iOS 27.2 after being pulled from iOS 27 beta

Throughout the iOS 27 beta this summer, one of my favorite AI features was a Messages addition that didn’t feel like AI at all: Suggestions.

Here’s what they do, per Apple:

Messages offers one-tap suggestions based on the context of users’ conversations, making it easier than ever to get things done, such as creating a reminder or a note. For example, if someone asks for photos, Messages can also help users find the right ones, recognizing keywords, locations, and people in their library to find the best options.

Suggestions appear as small, convenient action buttons beneath messages they’re relevant to.

As seen in the image below, if someone asks you to do something, you might see a suggestion to add to Reminders or Notes. Or if an event is mentioned, suggestions lets you easily add it to your calendar.

Suggestions worked well for me in the iOS 27 beta, but shortly before the public launch last month, Apple delayed the feature into a “future software update.”

Now in iOS 27.2, suggestions have officially returned, launching for all users. And one way they’ve changed might explain why they were pulled in the first place.

As I mentioned, suggestions performed as expected for me during the summer. But if I had one complaint, it was that they sometimes appeared when a message’s context didn’t merit them. At times I saw suggestions to add things to Notes, Reminders, or Calendar when there wasn’t a clear justification for these recommendations.

But in iOS 27.2, I’ve seen far fewer suggestions appearing in my Messages conversations. When I see them, it’s always obvious why they’re being offered. Clearly the feature benefited from a little extra fine tuning.

If you want even more control over the types of Suggestions that appear, you can manually configure categories under Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages ⇾ Suggested Actions.

title: RAMageddon is ready to rage on through 2030
snippet: SK Hynix, one of the major companies behind memory production, says that it’s sold out through 2029, leaving RAMageddon ready to rage on for at least the next three years. more…
fullText:
SK Hynix, one of the major companies behind memory production, says that it’s sold out through 2029, leaving RAMageddon ready to rage on for at least the next three years.

On its latest earnings call today, SK Hynix confirmed that production of both DRAM and HBM (high-bandwidth memory) are effectively sold out not just for this year, not just for next year, but through 2029. That puts RAMageddon, the global shortage of memory, lasting at least another three years before we see any relief.

SK Hynix’s CFO explains (via The Motley Fool, Seeking Alpha):

…memory supply cannot keep pace with this level of demand growth, thus, we expect it to be difficult to fully meet customers’ volume requirements in the near term, given the complexities involved in implementing leading-edge processes and the lead times required to construct new production facilities. A situation where supply cannot keep up with demand is expected to persist for some time, a constraint projected to continue through 2030.

Micron, one of the other companies responsible for memory production, previously said to expect 2027 to be “even tighter” compared to 2026. 

	

The SK Hynix call also details how the company is making long-term agreements which already account for “more than 50% of our total capacity for 2027 and 2028.”

SK Hynix isn’t the biggest name in DRAM/HBM production, with Samsung accounting for a larger share, but everyone else is dealing with the same constraints. PCMag points out that SK Hynix is working to build out more production capacity, as everyone else is too, but it takes time to build out the complex infrastructure.

Buckle up folks, this isn’t ending anytime soon. 🫠

title: The Ultrahuman Ring Pro Hits US Shelves Amid Oura Lawsuit
snippet: It’s available online and in select stores, so you can check out the smart ring in person.
fullText:
Ultrahuman hasn’t had an easy time getting its smart rings into the US, but on Wednesday, it announced that the Ring Pro is officially available for purchase on the Best Buy, Target, Walmart and Ultrahuman websites and in 300 Best Buy stores. In the coming weeks, it will roll out in over 1,000 Target and Walmart stores. 

Priced at $479, the Ring Pro requires no extra subscription to track heart rate, heart rate variability, skin temperature, sleep, movement, stress, recovery and your circadian rhythm. 

However, this launch comes just six days after competitor Oura filed a patent infringement complaint against Ultrahuman, seeking to ban its ring in the US.

			

More from CNET

A previous ban in the US

Oura was actually successful in getting Ultrahuman’s smart ring, then the Ring Air, banned in the US in August 2025, following a US International Trade Commission ruling after Oura filed a patent infringement complaint with the ITC in March 2024. This was for patents that were not included in the most recent filing. 

Ultrahuman later globally unveiled its Ring Pro in February and received US Customs and Border Protection clearance one month later, making its smart ring available for preorder in the US. In May, the company also launched a Kickstarter campaign with the Ring Pro at up to 43% off.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro in aster black.Ultrahuman

The Ring Pro’s pros and cons

CNET Principal Writer Vanessa Hand Orellana has been testing the Ring Pro for months. “Its main advantage is its no subscription setup. All the main features aren’t behind a paywall like with Oura,” she said. “Also, the Ring Pro’s battery life up to 15 days is twice that of other smart rings.”

Some downsides include the Ring Pro being thicker than the Oura Ring 5 and more prone to scratches. The auto-workout detection needs work, and unless you pair it with a third-party device, the heart rate readings during workouts aren’t reliable. 

The Ring Pro offers up to 250 days of on-device health data storage, so you don’t need to constantly sync it with your phone. It comes with a one-year warranty and a Pro Charging Case that extends the combined battery life to at least 45 days and on-device storage up to one year. 

There is also Ultrahuman’s AI health and wellness assistant, Jade, which can take your health data and provide personalized guidance and insights. However, you should always exercise caution when trusting any company or AI agent with your health information. 

While the Ring Pro is subscription-less, there are optional add-ons called PowerPlugs that can track your respiratory health, cycle and ovulation, vitamin D, headaches and more. Some are free, while others cost up to $6.90 per month. 

The Ring Pro comes in sizes five to 13 and four colors: bionic gold, space silver, aster black and raw titanium. 

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is also available in raw titanium.Ultrahuman

The Ring Pro’s future in the US

On Tuesday, an Ultrahuman spokesperson told CNET in an email that, as the court hasn’t ruled on Oura’s latest complaint, the company plans to continue manufacturing and selling its Ring Pro in the US. 

“We will address Oura’s newly asserted claims through the appropriate legal process and will defend our position vigorously,” the spokesperson said.

title: Major Even Realities G2 smart glasses update adds Conversate ‘Pro Mode,’ Knowledge Base
snippet: Even Realities today announced that a new software version will be rolling out to the G2 smart glasses, complete with a personal knowledge base that, thankfully, only remembers what you tell it. more…
fullText:
Even Realities today announced that a new software version will be rolling out to the G2 smart glasses, complete with a personal knowledge base that, thankfully, only remembers what you tell it.

When the G2 smart glasses launched, Even Realities packed them with features aimed at professionals, as well as tech geeks who appreciate retro mixing with the modern. But features like Conversate can be valuable to anyone in the right situation.

Even Realities says Conversate is getting an overhauled “Pro Mode” that pulls data from something it’s calling Knowledge Base – a feature that remembers the information and data you select. These feature refreshes are included in the Even Realities G2 version 2.4.0 update, which also upgrades the company’s AI interface to Even AI 2.0.

In order, it works like this:

	

Files and audio recorded in Conversate mode on the Even Realities G2 glasses, along with any manually uploaded files, sync to a secure Google Cloud Platform server in the EU.

Knowledge Base updates your information to disseminate.

Even AI 2.0 and active Conversate sessions pull context from the Knowledge Base.

Even Realities allows users to select up to 10 Conversate records to upload to that context tree during the initial setup. More can be added as they’re recorded. It also seems that new Conversate sessions need to be selected for upload and won’t be added to that database automatically, unless the user toggles automated uploads on.

Whatever data is there, Conversate Pro Mode will surface during relevant sessions. For instance, if you’re a sports journalist and have a backlog of recorded meetings in Conversate, new instances will provide context based on what you already know. It’s a more trustworthy approach than letting an AI model surface information it thinks is relevant. Even AI won’t stop doing that, but the Knowledge Base might be a more palatable source for some.

The biggest part of this update comes down to Even AI 2.0. Even Realities says it’s a “major upgrade” to how users interact with the G2 glasses as a whole. In reality, it comes down to quality-of-life changes that should make the smart glasses easier to use.

The G2 glasses are now able to activate Even AI with the touch sensor. When you hold it down, the recording starts, but stops when you release. And instead of requiring a new wake word for a follow-up, users can enable multi-turn conversations. Opening Even Hubs apps and changing certain settings right from the AI chat are supported, too.

Even Realities says Knowledge Base and Conversate Pro Mode will both launch today in beta. Because it’s still an early feature, it will be limited for users based on a monthly usage allowance. There’s no mention of pricing after beta in Even Realities’ press release.

Oh, and there’s a new tortoiseshell color option.

title: Galaxy Z Fold 8 is still $200 off as iPhone Duo displays crack
snippet: Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 has the same form factor as Apple’s new iPhone Duo, but it’s in stock, discounted, and doesn’t have any cracking display issue at the moment. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 has the same form factor as Apple’s new iPhone Duo, but it’s in stock, discounted, and doesn’t have any cracking display issue at the moment.

Apple’s first foldable is turning heads right now as many are considering buying a foldable for the first time. And rightly so. The iPhone Duo has a compact form factor, useful inner display, and good attention to detail in its software, and early reviews largely praise the device.

iPhone Duo review roundup: The same problems Android foldables face, but with Apple’s polish

But, now that it’s actually starting to ship, some customers have found that the inner display is facing a problem. While Apple hasn’t confirmed any major issues, it seems that there’s a hinge component that’s causing problems and, ultimately, causing the inner display to “crack” with green lines stemming from the center of the screen.

iPhone Duo displays are breaking, and you’re not folding it wrong

Not fun! 

	

Meanwhile, Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 shares the iPhone Duo’s same form factor (but thinner and way lighter), has excellent software, and was an absolute pleasure to use when we reviewed it earlier this year, all while display issues like this have not been reported in any capacity. 

And it’s just $1,699 right now.

Where the iPhone Duo starts at $2,000, Samsung has been discounting its popular foldable by $200 or more as of late. So, if you’ve been looking to buy a foldable for the first time, it’s at least worth a look.

title: iOS 27.3 release date: Here’s when to expect new iPhone features
snippet: Apple released iOS 27.2 this week with new features for Messages, Siri AI, and Photos, plus an Apple Music rebrand and more. But work on iOS 27.3 is already well underway, here’s when to expect the next big iPhone update. more…
fullText:
Apple released iOS 27.2 this week with new features for Messages, Siri AI, and Photos, plus an Apple Music rebrand and more. But work on iOS 27.3 is already well underway, here’s when to expect the next big iPhone update.

iOS 27.3 is almost available in beta, with public launch expected in mid-December

If you follow Apple closely, the company’s software release patterns quickly become clear.

For example, iOS 27.2 launched this week right around the same time as Apple’s previous releases in years past.

The only difference is that normally we would have expected iOS 27.1 in the last week of October rather than 27.2. But due to Apple making iOS 27.1 exclusive to iPhone Duo, all software releases for the iOS 27 cycle will be off by one number—despite following the same timing as ever.

That means iOS 27.3 is up next, and its release should align with historic patterns for x.2 updates.

iOS 27.3 is expected to arrive in beta within the next few days—Monday, November 2 is likely.

As for the public launch, here’s what past years have shown for comparable x.2 updates:

iOS 26.2: Friday, December 12

iOS 18.2: Wednesday, December 11

iOS 17.2: Monday, December 11

Based on this pattern, iOS 27.3 is expected to release in mid-December.

Apple always tries to ship its last software update of the year with a little buffer before taking a holiday break. That way if any major issues arise, the company can develop a quick fix and push it out before much of the company takes time off.

As for new iPhone features in iOS 27.3, we’ll know a lot more after the beta arrives. So far though, at a minimum we’re expecting the additional Siri AI languages Apple announced this week, plus the return of the all-new Health app.

Will you install the iOS 27.3 beta or wait for the release version? Let us know in the comments.

fullText:

Google’s most gorgeous thermostat is ready to get you saving money this winter, and I don’t just mean because of this great deal. If you have an older Nest thermostat or have been looking to upgrade to Nest this year, now’s the ideal time thanks to this $60-off Nest Thermostat 4th-gen deal.

Nest Thermostat 4th-gen deal at Amazon

This is the lowest price we’ve seen in a bit for the latest thermostat in Google’s lineup, nearly matching last year’s Black Friday low, and it also includes a Nest Temperature Sensor (2nd gen) that you can put somewhere else in your home to help the thermostat better regulate the temperature across your house. Ideally, this sensor would go in a room that’s always hotter or colder than the rest of the house (we all have one of those, right?).

Google launched the 4th-gen Nest Learning Thermostat in fall 2024 after a solid decade of no hardware updates to the “Learning Thermostat” line. My particular 3rd-gen Learning Thermostat came out way back in 2015, and while Google has been good about supporting it over the years, I imagine the clock is ticking for end-of-life support pretty soon. The first two generations lost support in 2025.

	

The new design is doggone gorgeous, with a very Pixel Watch-like design that comes in three fantastic colors: Silver, Gold, and Obsidian. All three colors are polished like they just came out of a jewelry store and look stunning even in the most boring hallway. Aside from its good looks, this one packs Google Home and Gemini smarts, a new Dynamic Farsight feature powered by Soli, the rotating bezel everyone loves, Smart Ventilation air quality measurement, and a ton of other great features in the Google Home app.

This model doesn’t require a C-wire to function, so it’s compatible with a ton of HVAC systems and includes an easy step-by-step guide within the Google Home app to get you started. Don’t worry, I have zero electrical wiring experience, and I got mine hooked up right the first time, so be sure to upgrade to this Nest Thermostat 4th-gen deal today and get to saving money with Gemini smarts this winter.

title: XREAL Aura debuts with 150 made-for-XR experiences, including Project Hail Mary, NBA, Fallout, and more
snippet: XREAL Aura already works with all your favorite Android apps thanks to Android XR, and that includes over 150 experiences that tap into the power of the XR glasses. more…
fullText:
XREAL Aura already works with all your favorite Android apps thanks to Android XR, and that includes over 150 experiences that tap into the power of the XR glasses.

As I opened the NBA app on XREAL Aura and tapped the tabletop option, I watched the coffee table in front of me transform into a basketball court, complete with models of each player moving around the court in real-time. It was as if I were a giant looking in through the top of the arena. Not only could I get as close or as far away as I wanted, but all the game’s important stats were right there for me to peruse. The video below is taken from the Apple Vision Pro, but the experience is similar on XREAL Aura.

It was one of the most convincing reasons I’ve seen to own a pair of legit smart glasses, and the very reason XREAL chose to launch with Google’s Android XR at its core. All your favorite Android apps are here and work exactly as you hoped, and a curated selection of 150 now delivers a real sense of presence to the heart and soul of each app’s experience.

Save $200 on XREAL Aura now

But it’s not just about compatibility or interoperability, either. The reach of Google’s Android platform means that big names like NBA, NASCAR, the San Francisco Ballet Company, Hulu, Netflix, Disney+, and so many more are playable in-glasses on day one, many with bespoke XR experiences.

	

Gamers will also be excited to know that Fallout is making a return in Fallout: Factions, a new strategy title for two players that brings classic units to a new tabletop experience. Then, there’s Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars, an original mixed reality game with a story that takes place during the weeks Rocky and Ryland Grace spent trying to survive in space in the untold section of the novel (and movie) during the journey to Eridani.

Acclaimed actor and director Andy Serkis is even in on the mix with Nevatars, an Android XR exclusive that follows a character artist’s abandoned digital creations and will be free for the first 6 months. And then there’s Asteroid, a new type of immersive film from Doug Liman that takes the cinematic storytelling of a movie and meshes it with interactive gameplay via live conversational AI (Gemini). This one’s exclusive to Android XR and free for XREAL Aura owners.

Some of the most popular VR developers are also on board, including Resolution Games, who returns with a fresh port of the D&D-like strategy game, Demeo, plus the Android XR-exclusive Holochess (which is already on the Play Store). Holochess transforms the normally turn-based chess rules into a real-time strategy battle of Clankers vs. Xenoswarm, all on the table right in front of you. This 2-player game is free-to-play, and a third faction can be unlocked for $2.99.

There are also a ton of spatial games and experiences to play, as well as. Simply Piano XR merges physical instruments with virtual ones, giving you a real-time way to learn and improve your music skills while wearing your glasses. And that’s just the tip of the iceberg as developers continue to branch out with new, creative ways of using spatial computing devices like XREAL Aura.

title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro Hands-On: Apple Finally Lets Us Swipe the Screen
snippet: A great-sounding display, but Apple seems out of touch for the touchscreen.
fullText:
Surpassed only by the iPhone Duo, this year’s most anticipated Apple announcement is its launch of both a 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen display — the company’s last-to-the-party use of both technologies in one of its laptops. And despite the awful “PROLED” name, it’s more than just a fancy new display. It’s a complete design overhaul that, at least on paper, brings its feature set up to the front of the class for professional content creation, albeit with the same processor options and ports as the other MacBook Pros.

Aside from a screen that brings its capabilities more in line with the Studio Display XDR, the new model adds:

Touch support 

The iPhone’s Dynamic Island

A 16TB configuration

Improved speakers with Dolby Atmos support and better mic

A thinner and lighter design

Genlock support

It doesn’t come cheap, though; as predicted, you pay a $400 premium over the standard models. The 14-inch M5 Pro model starts at $2,899 compared with $2,499 for the same non-OLED version, and the M5 Max model begins at $4,499 compared with $4,099. If you want to upgrade to 16TB, you have to bump to the M5 Max — that’s a minimum buy-in of $11,499 with only 36GB of memory. Preorders started on Wednesday, and systems are slated to start shipping Nov. 6.

		

			

One of the most popular changes won’t be the whizzy features, but the drop in weight to 3 pounds for the 14-inch model (down from 3.4 pounds) and to 4 pounds (down from 4.7 pounds) for the 16-inch. Also, while Apple updated its sound system to deliver better bass and incorporated Dolby Atmos support to its spatial audio, one of the more notable enhancements is the claimed improvements to the sound when the MacBook is closed. 

Hands-on impressions from Executive Producer Bridget Carey 

From my brief moments with the laptop, I can tell the touchscreen is something you may use as a supplemental feature — a quick zoom here, a drag-and-drop there. But even if you don’t see yourself needing to poke a screen, the vibrant OLED display is a noticeable leap in quality. 

I was expecting to see rows of smudged up screens on demo tables. Yes, there are plenty of Apple staff with polishing cloths to give it a quick buff between tests, but my screens were not looking too smudged up after dragging my fingers around. It’s also less reflective — so those true blacks can be enjoyed without light reflections getting in the way.

I got a chance to see Apple’s display side by side with another Windows OLED Touchscreen, the Lenovo Yoga 9i. It was no contest — the new MacBook Pro was far superior with a more vibrant display, and it kept the detail even in extremely bright light, plus it was less reflective. 

Apple brought back the illuminated logo on the cover.Bridget Carey/CNET

I was worried it might be a little hard to control certain aspects of MacOS with a clumsy finger, but it was able to accurately pick up on my touch. Controls would enlarge when I wanted to screen or expand a window, to make sure I pressed what I intended, and I quickly got used to dragging and locking windows to the sides. You have to do it with a little swivel in your hips and a flick of the wrist.

An impressive screen

A lot of the traditional advantages of OLED over alternatives like IPS with array backlights — such as a wider color gamut and true blacks — are less pronounced than they used to be. 

That’s even more true for the current MacBook Pro’s mini-LED-backlit Liquid Retina XDR screens: They already deliver excellent deep blacks and 100% P3 gamut coverage, along with great color accuracy sufficient for prosumer creative work. 

But the PROLED XDR screen sounds top-notch. While I take Apple’s claim of a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio with 10,000,000 grains of salt — the arithmetic ratio of peak brightness to minimum black isn’t really meaningful, especially beyond about a million — the display has an expanded gamut that covers the Adobe RGB color space and more of Rec. 2020, a space for mastering video. 

The latter is still only 80%, but at the moment, that’s the best you can get in a laptop display.

Tara Brown/CNET

Peak brightness is also similar to the desktop display at 2,000 nits. As with the current screens, though, you can set the SDR brightness only up to 1,000 nits; above that, it’s automated to compensate only for bright sunlight. That can get frustrating for people like me who find auto- brightness distracting.

 The display can do 1,000 nits full screen in both SDR and HDR, though. Microsoft’s recently shipped Surface Laptop Ultra also hits 2,000 nits, the first Windows laptop that does, but uses mini-LED.

Oddly, Apple still quotes a 1-nit minimum brightness spec, similar to its mini-LED screens, though OLED’s native minimum is a lot lower: Theoretically, it’s zero, but professional colorimeters have measured it a lot lower. That may be because Apple has adopted it as a standard, and possibly clamped it, to tonally match its mini-LED models.

Apple also refers to its panel technology generically as “tandem OLED,” which is a little annoying, since there is a raft of tandem OLED types. But it is “state of the art!”

The letdowns

There are a couple of potential disappointments, though. For one, the battery life is unchanged. While the MacBook Pro’s battery life has always been good, it’s clear that the OLED display didn’t provide any power savings, or at least savings that weren’t spent elsewhere in the system.

Touch looks like the biggest mixed bag, though. The hardware is only a small aspect of the implementation; operating system interfaces like those of iOS and iPadOS are built around considerations like your finger is bigger and fatter than a cursor. Simply porting the mobile interfaces to a laptop isn’t necessarily a solution, either. 

Playing a keyboard on a touchscreen that can’t open wide? Bridget Carey (that’s her hand) says, “You should not play piano like a doofus, finger stabbing the screen.”Tara Brown/CNET

We use laptops in part because a hardware keyboard is sometimes the best input choice, and even navigating the mobile devices via touch can get annoying, so those interfaces don’t necessarily translate optimally.

The point is, a lot is riding on how Apple has adapted MacOS for touch. For instance, the Touch Bar floundered in part because it felt grafted on rather than integral to the OS’ interface, as well as arguably superfluous. 

And since Apple didn’t launch the capability with MacOS 27 at its developer conference, WWDC, this year, it sounds like the applications will be behind. That’s not something you beta test on a pro-level production system. Pros rely heavily on muscle memory. It should really have launched with a MacBook Air. 

Plus, to adapt to touchscreen use, Apple had to stiffen the hinge — poking the screen makes that necessary — and add image stabilization to the webcam in case you poke the screen during video calls.

Apple seemed like it was really stretching to find meaningful uses for touch. Playing piano on a screen that forces your hand to an awkward angle? No thanks. The one application that sounded like it might be OK was for developers to simulate mobile app interfaces.

I was also kind of hoping for increased refresh rates beyond 120Hz or the ability to manually set it above 60Hz. Apple seems to position ProMotion as a power-saving technology rather than for gaming. Apple also seems to think 60fps is a great frame rate, so it’s not surprising.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Bridget Carey
						

						

							Editor at Large						
					

											

								

											Bridget Carey is an award-winning consumer technology reporter and host of the weekly Apple show, "One More Thing."

title: Instagram takes on YouTube with new 90-minute horizontal video format
snippet: According to The Hollywood Reporter, Instagram today began testing a new long-form horizontal video format with select creators in the U.S. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
According to The Hollywood Reporter, Instagram today began testing a new long-form horizontal video format with select creators in the U.S. Here are the details.

Instagram doubles down on long-form horizontal video

Every now and again, Instagram tries to go after YouTube with a new product. IGTV, for instance, was one of the social network’s attempts at competing in the long-form video space.

However, IGTV never really took off, and Instagram eventually phased it out as it shifted its focus to Reels.

Today, as reported by THR, Instagram kicked off a new attempt to compete with YouTube with Features, a new format that supports horizontal videos up to 90 minutes long.

Aimed at podcasters and other long-form creators, the feature has already been tested in Brazil and is now expanding to select creators in the U.S. It also lets them link shorter Reels to their full-length videos.

From THR:

Starting Monday, Instagram will be launching a test of horizontal videos of up to 90 minutes with select creators in the U.S. The product, called Features, is aimed at podcasters, comedians and other longform creators, with the ability to refer viewers to the full video from the shortform reels on the platform, which are typically around three minutes or less.

The move comes at a time when social media feeds and recommendations are increasingly filled with short clips from stand-up comedy performances and video podcasts, giving users snippets of much longer shows and episodes.

With Features, Instagram seems to be looking to capitalize on that trend, turning those clips into a gateway to full-length episodes.

According to THR, which spoke with Instagram VP of Product Tessa Lyons, the full-length videos will also be recommended to users on the Explore page and in other parts of the app.

Lyons told THR that users will be able to tap on a podcast clip in Reels to continue watching or jump straight to the full episode, without leaving Instagram.

Here’s Lyons elaborating on how Instagram plans to help creators monetize their long-form videos:

“For established creators who already have those relationships, they can bring that content with those placements and that branded content. And we also think that there’s a big opportunity for us to help creators who don’t yet have that infrastructure and that business behind them.”

THR notes that the move is part of the entertainment industry’s broader push into video podcasts, with companies like Netflix and Disney also bringing creator content to their platforms to compete with YouTube.

Instagram, meanwhile, has also expanded its Instagram for TV app to Apple TV in the U.S., and Features is now expected to play a role in the company’s broader push to leverage podcasts and other long-form videos to keep viewers engaged across devices.

title: Instagram tests ‘Features’ long-form videos, but missing YouTube’s ad share for now
snippet: Instagram is launching “Features” as its first real dive into long-form video content in what could be a real rival to YouTube, though Instagram is, for now, missing an alternative to YouTube’s ad share setup for creators. more…
fullText:
Instagram is launching “Features” as its first real dive into long-form video content in what could be a real rival to YouTube, though Instagram is, for now, missing an alternative to YouTube’s ad share setup for creators.

In a 6-minute video shared today, Instagram head Adam Mosseri and VP Tessa Lyons explain “Features,” a new effort to bring long-form, horizontal video content to Instagram. “Features” allow creators to expand on content in Reels, using short-form video to build up an audience for longer-form content. 

Mosseri explains:

Sat down with @tessalyonsss to talk about why we’re investing in longer videos, which we’re going to call Features, and how they fit with Reels, Series, Live and TV. It’s early, and we’re testing and listening to feedback as we go. But we’re excited to give creators more room to tell their stories with the communities they’ve already built here. More to come.

The video starts with Mosseri admitting that he’s been “against doing long-form video on Instagram,” but the two go on to explain how the trend of friends watching Reels together, including on TV apps, pushed towards this expansion to long-form, horizontal content. Examples of podcast or comedy clips being used in Reels with longer episodes or specials available on “Features” is mentioned, with the two formats being able to connect to each other. 

	

The Hollywood Reporter adds that this is US-only to start – the announcement video can’t even be viewed outside of the US, we found – and also that Instagram will carry over “existing ad deals” with creators.

A lack of any mention around ad sharing programs on Instagram’s part immediately flooded the comments of the announcement, with users asking why they should post long-form videos on Instagram when YouTube pays creators for the same practice. Tessa Lyons says that Instagram thinks “there’s a big opportunity for us to help creators who don’t yet have that infrastructure and that business behind them,” but made no mention of a program like YouTube offers.

title: Spotify confirms it won’t stop Family Plan sharing verification, but it’s not a ‘crackdown’
snippet: Earlier this week a new method of Spotify Family plan verification came to light and, in its latest earnings call, Spotify says that it’s not a “crackdown,” but also something that doesn’t have an “end date.” more…
fullText:
Earlier this week a new method of Spotify Family plan verification came to light and, in its latest earnings call, Spotify says that it’s not a “crackdown,” but also something that doesn’t have an “end date.”

Like virtually every family sharing subscription, Spotify requires Family Plan members to be in the same physical household, but the music streaming app has been looser in its requirements and enforcement. A new method, though, started popping up recently in the form of a verification QR code that makes it a bit more difficult for remote participants to complete verification, and also threatens to ban users from Family plans for a full year if verification isn’t completed.

Spotify’s ‘QR code verification’ cracks down on sharing and could ban you for a year

Today, Spotify’s Q3 earnings call included a question about Spotify “beginning to crack down on Family Plan subscribers that do not live in the same home.” 

Responding to this, Spotify co-CEO Alex Norström says that this is not a “crackdown,” but a “routine improvement of our verification methods,” and something that Spotify will continue to work on. “This is not something that has an end date,” he said:

	

…this is not as much a crackdown as it is actually a routine improvement of our verification methods for our Family Plan. Family Plan has existed for a long while. It has been around for, I think it is now close to 12, 13 years in Spotify history, and it makes up a pretty significant proportion of our subscriber base. As such, it is important for us to just make sure over time that we improve the verification methods that we have. There are certainly ways, over time, to find holes around it. As that happens, we figure out how to improve it over time. This is not something that has an end date. This is not an implementation that is going to complete. This is just ongoing routine.

Reading between the lines, this is saying that Spotify isn’t going to be backing down from verification methods on its Family Plan sharing. QR codes are only the latest implementation.
